messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 60

Mr. R is a 64-year-old man who has worked in the same warehouse for nearly twenty years. He loads boxes onto pallets, checks inventory sheets, and keeps his head down. He has been married to his wife for thirty-five years, and they live in a quiet suburban home. He does not speak about what happened to him before he came to this country.

He remembers the morning it began. It was 1983. He was a university student in his hometown, walking to a bus stop when armed men pulled him into a van. For the next nine months, he was held in a concrete room with no windows. The men were from a faction fighting the government, and they accused him of being a spy. They kept his hands bound, his eyes covered, and they questioned him for hours at a time. He learned to listen for footsteps, for the creak of the door, for the sound of a key turning. He learned that begging only made them hit harder. He learned to make his mind very small, to focus on the pattern of water dripping in the corner, to count the seconds between each drop.

When he was finally released—in a trade, he was told, though he never understood the details—he weighed less than a hundred pounds. His family found him walking along a dirt road. He did not cry. He did not explain. He went back to school, finished his degree, and married the woman his mother had chosen for him. He told his wife a shortened version of the story: "Some bad men held me for a while, but it's over." She never pressed him for more.

They moved to the United States in the early 1990s, and Mr. R found work at the warehouse. He is reliable. He never calls in sick. But his coworkers have noticed that he startles easily. One day a forklift backfired in the shipping bay, and Mr. R dropped to the ground, covering his head with his arms. He stayed there for five minutes, unable to speak. The supervisor helped him to the break room, and Mr. R said it was just a headache. He has never told anyone at work the truth.

At home, he sleeps in a separate room from his wife. The bedroom door must be open, but the closet door must be closed. He checks the locks on every window three times before bed. He cannot stand the sound of keys jingling—it makes his chest tighten and his palms sweat. He avoids television shows about war or prisons. When his wife asks him to go to a family gathering, he often agrees, then finds an excuse at the last minute. He says he is tired. He says his back hurts from lifting boxes. He says he doesn't feel well. What he feels is a pressure behind his ribs, as if the room is collapsing inward. He has not told her about the nightmares: the same concrete wall, the same gag in his mouth, the same voice asking questions he cannot answer. He wakes gasping, and he lies still until the feeling passes.

His daughter, who lives in another state, calls every Sunday. He listens to her voice, but he forgets what she says moments after hanging up. He remembers the texture of the blindfold against his eyelids more clearly than the color of her eyes. Sometimes he wonders if he ever really left that room.

Last month, his wife found him standing in the bathroom at 3 A.M., staring at his reflection. When she asked what was wrong, he said, "Nothing." She has started to cry in the kitchen when she thinks he cannot hear. He knows she is worried, but he does not know how to give her the words. He has never said out loud that he still hears the footsteps. He has never said that the counting has never stopped.
